title: Late Payments Trap £26bn in Unpaid Invoices, Hitting 1.5m UK Firms
snippet: New analysis from Century Business Finance links overdue invoices to 14,000 UK business closures annually and an £11bn drag on the economy. The post Late Payments Trap £26bn in Unpaid Invoices, Hitting 1.5m UK Firms appeared first on The Fintech Times.
fullText:
Late payments remain a structural threat to UK small business survival, with an estimated £26 billion locked in overdue invoices at any one time, according to new analysis published by loan broker Century Business Finance. The firm’s research, drawn from Office for National Statistics, Companies House and government datasets, finds that around 1.5 million UK businesses, or 28% of the small business population, are affected by late payments each year.

The headline figure the report places on the problem is stark: late payments are estimated to contribute to approximately 14,000 business closures annually, equivalent to 38 companies ceasing operations every day. The aggregate cost to the broader UK economy is put at almost £11 billion per year.

The behavioural trap

Ben Larkins, co-founder of Century Business Finance

Perhaps the most telling finding is not the scale of overdue debt but the reluctance to recover it. One in three small businesses does not formally pursue late payments, the analysis found, citing a desire to protect customer relationships. That dynamic is well understood in trade credit markets but rarely quantified at this level: the fear of losing a client routinely outweighs the financial damage of carrying unpaid invoices, at least until the cash position deteriorates sharply.

Ben Larkins, co-founder of Century Business Finance, said: “Late payments aren’t just frustrating, they can prevent otherwise healthy businesses from paying staff, covering day-to-day costs or investing in future growth. Allowing unpaid invoices to build up often creates much bigger financial pressures in the long run.”

Century also published a regional breakdown using late-payment incidence rates from the Q1 2026 Business Health Report published by insolvency trade body R3, scaled against SME population data. The West Midlands recorded the highest rate at 2,625 late payments per 100 SMEs, followed by Scotland at 2,135 and Yorkshire and Humber at 1,373. Greater London, often assumed to carry the heaviest commercial stress, ranked sixth at 1,138 per 100 SMEs. Northern Ireland recorded the lowest rate at 431.

Regulatory and market context

The late-payments problem sits against a backdrop of intermittent government attempts to tighten the regime. The UK Prompt Payment Code, administered through the Small Business Commissioner, sets a 30-day payment standard for public sector contracts and a 60-day ceiling for the private sector, but compliance and enforcement have long been criticised as inadequate. Successive consultations have discussed mandatory reporting, stronger penalties and extending the Commissioner’s powers, but legislative progress has been slow.

At the product level, the gap between the scale of overdue trade receivables and the availability of invoice finance remains commercially significant. Invoice factoring and asset-based lending are established tools, but adoption among micro and small enterprises is limited, partly due to cost and partly due to unfamiliarity. Open finance infrastructure, which in principle allows lenders to assess receivables and cash-flow data in near real time, creates the conditions for more granular, dynamic working-capital products. Several UK fintechs and challenger banks have moved into embedded invoice-finance rails, though penetration among businesses below the £1 million revenue threshold remains modest.

Century Business Finance has also launched a free SME Cash Flow MOT tool alongside the research, a self-assessment resource the company says helps businesses evaluate their financial health and prepare for growth. The firm operates as a loan broker rather than a direct lender, connecting SMEs with funding of between £10,000 and £250,000 from its panel of lenders.

The research is self-commissioned and serves as a marketing exercise for the broker. The underlying datasets it cites, ONS business population estimates and Companies House insolvency data, are publicly available and reputable, but the causal link between late payments and the 14,000 closure figure is an estimate rather than a direct attribution from official statistics.

title: SCRYPT Takes Licensed Stablecoin Settlement Into East Africa
snippet: Norman Wooding, co-founder and CEO of SCRYPT, on why Kenya, Tanzania, Rwanda and Uganda are the proving ground for licensed stablecoin settlement. The post SCRYPT Takes Licensed Stablecoin Settlement Into East Africa appeared first on The Fintech Times.
fullText:
SCRYPT, the Swiss digital asset infrastructure firm, announced on 13 July the expansion of its licensed stablecoin settlement infrastructure across four East African markets: Kenya, Tanzania, Rwanda and Uganda. The expansion gives banks, payment providers and corporate treasury teams a route from local currencies directly into stablecoins, without first sourcing US dollars through correspondent banking channels.

Norman Wooding, founder and CEO at SCRYPT

The Zurich-based firm provides trading, settlement and custody to institutional clients through a FINMA-licensed Swiss entity. Norman Wooding, its co-founder and CEO, has worked in digital assets since 2016 and is a former lecturer at the London School of Economics. He answered The Fintech Times’ written questions on the expansion.

Why East Africa, and why now? What makes Kenya, Tanzania, Rwanda and Uganda the right corridors for licensed stablecoin settlement?

Africa represents one of the clearest examples of where stablecoins are moving beyond speculation and becoming practical financial infrastructure. The demand is being driven by real economic needs: businesses need better ways to access dollar liquidity, manage treasury operations and move value across borders efficiently.

East Africa is particularly compelling because these markets combine growing digital adoption with increasingly connected economies and businesses that operate internationally. Companies across the region are engaging in cross-border commerce every day, but many still face friction when moving money through traditional financial systems.

What makes these corridors important is that the need already exists. Stablecoins are not creating a new behaviour; they are providing a more efficient layer for financial activity that is already happening. The opportunity is to bring licensed, institutional-grade infrastructure to support those flows.

For SCRYPT, this expansion is not simply about geographic growth. Africa is a strong proof point for our broader thesis: when financial systems face friction, businesses need reliable rails that allow them to move value faster, more transparently and with greater certainty. Stablecoins are increasingly becoming part of that stack.

What does moving directly from local currencies into stablecoins change for banks, payment providers and corporate treasuries in markets with constrained dollar liquidity?

The biggest change is removing unnecessary friction from the settlement process.

Today, many businesses operating across borders have to navigate multiple layers to complete international payments. They may need to source dollars through traditional banking channels, manage foreign exchange conversions and rely on correspondent banking networks that involve multiple intermediaries. Each additional step can introduce cost, delay and uncertainty.

By enabling direct pathways from local currencies into stablecoin settlement, businesses have a more efficient way to access dollar-denominated liquidity and move value internationally. For banks, payment providers and corporate treasury teams, this creates an additional financial rail that can complement existing infrastructure.

The important distinction is that stablecoins are not replacing the financial system. Banks and payment providers remain essential. What is changing is that businesses now have access to another settlement layer that can operate continuously and reduce friction where traditional systems struggle.

We have seen this shift globally: stablecoins started as a way to move between fiat and digital assets, but their real utility is increasingly emerging in payments, treasury management and settlement. The infrastructure is becoming the product.

How does a licensed, regulated stablecoin settlement layer differ from the informal crypto flows that already exist in these markets?

The difference is trust, operational resilience and accountability.

Digital assets have demonstrated their usefulness in many markets because they solve real problems around access, speed and value transfer. But businesses and financial institutions require much more than access to a digital asset. They need reliable counterparties, secure custody, transparent execution, operational controls and a framework they can confidently integrate into their existing financial processes.

That is where a licensed provider becomes critical. The next phase of digital asset adoption will not be driven by informal activity or speculation. It will be driven by businesses integrating digital assets into real workflows: payments, treasury management, liquidity operations and settlement.

At SCRYPT, our role is to provide the trusted foundation that enables businesses to do that confidently. We bring together trading, settlement and custody through a single licensed partner, giving organisations a secure and reliable way to integrate digital assets into their operations.

The broader shift we are seeing is that stablecoins are becoming less about crypto-native users and more about how money moves. The end user may never need to think about the underlying technology. They simply need a faster, more efficient and reliable way to move value.

What were the hardest regulatory and banking relationships to build for this expansion, and what did you learn?

Building a trusted financial network requires much more than technology. The hardest part is creating the foundation around that technology: ensuring strong licensing frameworks, establishing trusted banking relationships, developing robust operational processes and creating confidence among partners.

One of the biggest lessons we have learned is that institutional adoption depends on trust. Businesses are not looking for a short-term solution; they are looking for a trusted platform they can rely on as they scale their operations.

That means approaching digital assets with the same level of discipline expected from traditional financial services. Security, transparency, compliance and reliability are not optional: they are the foundation.

Another important lesson is that every market has different requirements. You cannot take a one-size-fits-all approach. Success requires understanding local currency dynamics, banking structures and the needs of businesses operating in those markets.

Ultimately, the opportunity is not just about introducing new technology. It is about building the bridges between digital assets and the existing financial system. That requires patience, strong partnerships and a long-term commitment to doing things properly.

What comes next for SCRYPT, and how big can stablecoin settlement in Africa become?

The opportunity is significant because the underlying demand is already clear. Businesses across Africa need better ways to manage cross-border payments, access liquidity and operate efficiently in markets where traditional systems can create friction.

For SCRYPT, this is not a future roadmap; our African settlement capabilities are already live today across four East African markets. Businesses and financial service providers can already access digital asset trading, settlement and custody through our FINMA-licensed Swiss entity, with active currency support across markets including Nigeria, Kenya, Tanzania, Uganda and Rwanda.

We believe the future of finance will be increasingly connected, digital and always-on. Stablecoins are a key part of that evolution because they provide a settlement layer that can operate globally and efficiently. Africa is one of the strongest examples of why this matters. The adoption story is not about speculation; it is about solving practical financial challenges. Businesses need reliable ways to move value, manage treasury and participate in the global economy.

We’ll continue building the capabilities that allow digital assets to become a trusted part of financial operations, not as a replacement for existing systems, but as a powerful extension of them.

title: Solaris Adds Instant-Access Savings Account to ADAC Credit Card Range
snippet: The Berlin-based BaaS bank is rolling out a Tagesgeldkonto to ADAC cardholders, offering a 3.5% promotional rate for three months before reverting to The post Solaris Adds Instant-Access Savings Account to ADAC Credit Card Range appeared first on The Fintech Times.
fullText:
Solaris, the Berlin-headquartered Banking-as-a-Service provider, has added an instant-access savings account to the ADAC credit card portfolio, extending a partnership that has grown steadily since Solaris took on the programme. The product, known in Germany as a Tagesgeldkonto, follows a soft launch in September that made it available to 50,000 ADAC cardholders ahead of the full portfolio rollout.

Steffen Jentsch, CEO at Solaris

The account sits alongside the existing credit card account and can be opened digitally in a few steps. Onboarding requires IBAN linking and two-factor authentication. Deposits and withdrawals are processed either via the ADAC credit card account or a designated reference account, and deposited funds remain available daily.

Joost Greve, managing director of ADAC Finanzdienste GmbH

At launch, new customers receive a promotional interest rate of 3.5% per annum for the first three months. After that, a variable standard rate of 1.5% per annum applies to balances up to 100,000 euros. Interest accrues monthly and can be tracked daily through the ADAC credit card app and online banking portal.

Steffen Jentsch, chief executive of Solaris, said the savings product was the “next logical step” in the partnership, with a stated aim of continuously expanding digital services for ADAC’s large membership base. Joost Greve, managing director of ADAC Finanzdienste GmbH, pointed to simple digital processes and security standards as the product’s defining priorities.

Expanding the embedded product suite

The savings account is not the only feature added to the ADAC card this year. Since May, cardholders have had access to a function called EuroAbruf, which allows customers to transfer up to 5,000 euros from their available credit limit directly to a personal bank account via SEPA Instant Credit Transfer. The process is fully self-service and subject to risk and authorisation checks. According to a survey cited by Solaris, 90.3% of participating cardholders said they were very satisfied with the additional card features, though the methodology and sample size were not disclosed.

The two additions together represent a pattern familiar in embedded finance: a card product used as a distribution anchor, with savings, credit access and payments layered progressively on top. This approach deepens the cardholder relationship and increases product revenue per user without requiring a full banking app relaunch.

Market and regulatory context

Solaris holds a full German banking licence, which gives it the regulatory standing to offer deposit-taking products directly rather than relying on a separate bank partner. That distinction matters in a sector where several BaaS competitors operate as technology layers over a licensed bank, creating additional counterparty risk and compliance complexity. The German deposit guarantee scheme (Einlagensicherungsfonds) applies to deposits held at Solaris, which will be relevant to any ADAC cardholder weighing the savings product against alternatives.

The competitive backdrop for BaaS-embedded savings is also developing quickly. Across Europe, several embedded-finance platforms and challenger banks have introduced savings products as a means of widening net interest margin, particularly at a time when central bank rate cycles have made deposit economics more attractive than they were for most of the low-rate decade. The promotional rate of 3.5% positions the ADAC product above the standard variable rate but below the leading easy-access rates available on the open market from specialist savings platforms, meaning ADAC cardholders who are already inside the app ecosystem are the primary target rather than active rate-shoppers.

The next milestone to watch is whether Solaris and ADAC Finanzdienste extend the product set further, potentially into investment or lending products, as the embedded suite deepens.

title: AFC Backs OCC and FDIC Moves to Reform Supervisory Data-Sharing Rules
snippet: The US fintech trade body wants regulators to allow banks and fintechs to share confidential supervisory information earlier in partnership due diligence. The post AFC Backs OCC and FDIC Moves to Reform Supervisory Data-Sharing Rules appeared first on The Fintech Times.
fullText:
The American Fintech Council (AFC) has filed comment letters with the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) and the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation (FDIC) backing proposed rule changes that would widen the circumstances under which banks and fintech companies can share confidential supervisory information (CSI). The letters respond to Notices of Proposed Rulemaking from both agencies and build on earlier AFC advocacy submitted jointly with the Independent Bank for Cooperatives Alliance to the OCC, FDIC and Federal Reserve in January 2026.

At its core, the AFC’s position is that the existing CSI framework creates friction at exactly the wrong moment in a bank-fintech relationship: before a formal partnership is established. Under current rules, institutions examining prospective partners, senior hires or acquisition targets face constraints that limit what supervisory context can be shared and with whom. The AFC argues that this effectively forces parties into a roundabout information-exchange process it describes as “playing a game of telephone,” increasing due diligence risk rather than reducing it.

What the AFC is asking for

Phil Goldfeder, CEO at AFC

The council is pressing both agencies on three related fronts. First, it wants the business-purpose disclosure authority that already permits some CSI sharing to be extended across the full life cycle of third-party relationships, including during initial pre-contractual due diligence. This would allow FDIC-examined service providers to disclose information about their own supervisory standing to prospective bank partners, enabling informed risk assessments before any contract is signed.

Second, in its OCC submission, the AFC specifically calls for CSI sharing to be permitted during merger and acquisition evaluations and during pre-engagement assessments of senior leadership candidates, covering a range of corporate events where supervisory history is directly material to decision-making.

Third, the AFC advocates for a structured route through which qualifying entities, including trade associations and independent research organisations, could receive institution-specific CSI solely to conduct aggregated analysis. The resulting aggregated findings would be publishable, supporting regulatory research and policy advocacy without exposing individual institution data.

On compliance safeguards, the AFC argues that protecting sensitive supervisory data does not require recreating the prior-approval burdens present in earlier frameworks. It recommends allowing confidentiality provisions to be embedded in existing commercial agreements rather than creating new standalone approval processes, and opposes rigid requirements such as domestic incorporation mandates, granular personnel access logs or transaction-level disclosures.

Phil Goldfeder, chief executive of the AFC, said a modern regulatory framework should allow institutions to exchange critical supervisory context at the earliest stages of collaboration, backed by rigorous compliance safeguards. Ian Moloney, the AFC’s chief policy officer, said modernising the framework would improve efficiency and efficacy in the examination process for all parties.

Regulatory context

The proposed OCC and FDIC rulemakings sit within a broader effort by US prudential regulators to update the legal infrastructure around bank-fintech partnerships. That effort has gathered pace following several high-profile partnership failures in the banking-as-a-service segment, where regulators found that banks had insufficient visibility into their fintech partners’ risk profiles before and during the relationship.

The CSI reform proposed here works the other side of that problem: not by adding oversight after a partnership is formed, but by improving the information available to both sides before they commit. For fintech companies that hold their own examination history from a prudential regulator, the ability to disclose that record to prospective bank partners could become a meaningful differentiator in a market where banks are increasingly cautious about onboarding new technology relationships without a full compliance picture. The comment period closes on the relevant regulatory deadlines; final rules, if adopted, would likely affect the majority of bank-fintech partnership frameworks operating under OCC and FDIC charters.

title: Porsche Targets 15% Operating Margin with 2035 Strategy Reset
snippet: Porsche's Sportwagenschmiede '35 plan targets a sub-200,000-unit break-even and a sixfold expansion of its bespoke Sonderwunsch programme. The post Porsche Targets 15% Operating Margin with 2035 Strategy Reset appeared first on The Fintech Times.
fullText:
Porsche AG has presented a nine-year strategic plan, branded Sportwagenschmiede ’35, at its Capital Markets Day at the Weissach Development Centre. The plan sets a long-term operating return on sales target of 15 per cent and an Automotive net cash flow margin of 12 per cent, with medium-term ambitions of 10 to 15 per cent and 9 to 12 per cent respectively. Group revenue is targeted at 41 to 45 billion euros in the medium term.

The centrepiece of the financial logic is a structural reduction in the break-even point to below 200,000 vehicles sold, achieved through a combination of workforce reduction, lower development costs and a shift toward higher-margin model segments. The company acknowledged that reaching the top end of its targets depends in part on an improved macroeconomic, geopolitical and regulatory environment.

Cost and workforce restructuring

Porsche has already enacted several disposals as part of its focus on core operations, including the sale of its stake in Rimac and Bugatti Rimac, an agreement to sell the MHP consulting subsidiary, and the planned closure of Cellforce Group, Porsche eBike Performance and Cetitec. A workforce reduction of 9,000 jobs has been agreed with employee representatives, alongside a job security commitment for the core workforce through 2035.

The company is targeting a 40 per cent reduction in management positions, a 25 to 30 per cent reduction in the overall workforce across direct and indirect functions, and a 30 per cent cut in production personnel costs. Development costs for future model lines are to fall by up to 20 per cent, supported by shorter development cycles and greater use of modular processes. Sales and distribution costs are earmarked for a 20 per cent reduction, partly through consolidating sales regions from five to four. Porsche Engineering and Porsche Digital will be merged into a single entity, Porsche Technologies.

Portfolio shift and new products

The product strategy is equally significant. Porsche is reducing model variants by around 20 per cent while increasing its presence in the higher-margin D and E segments, with a target of growing their share of the overall portfolio by approximately 45 per cent. The company confirmed the development of a mid-engined super sports car platform intended to sit above the 911, and is exploring a D-segment SUV positioned above the Cayenne. The electric 718 Boxster and Cayman are expected to contribute to sales from their first full production year in 2028, alongside a new B-segment SUV that will sit alongside the existing electric Macan.

The company also announced an increase in its stake in Manthey Racing GmbH to 67 per cent, and plans to scale its Sonderwunsch bespoke programme sixfold in revenue terms, framing individualisation as a structural margin lever rather than a boutique add-on. Average selling prices on top-of-range models are targeted to rise by around 20 per cent in the medium term.

Market and investor context

Dr Michael Leiters, CEO at Porsche AG

The Sportwagenschmiede ’35 announcement arrives at a difficult moment for premium automotive manufacturers broadly. Porsche’s own sales volumes have come under pressure, particularly in China, a market the company explicitly cited as a conservative planning assumption in its break-even modelling. Wider luxury auto peers have also been managing the cost and timing risks of electric vehicle transition alongside softening demand in key Asian markets.

The shift toward fewer, higher-priced and more personalised models is a defensible response to those pressures, drawing Porsche closer to the operating logic of ultra-luxury manufacturers such as Ferrari, which has long prioritised revenue-per-unit over volume. The risk is execution: restructuring 9,000 roles, cutting development timelines and simultaneously launching multiple new model lines in premium segments is a high-complexity programme. Investors will be watching whether the profitability targets hold if the China recovery is slower than even the conservative base case allows.

Chief executive Dr Michael Leiters framed the plan in operational terms: “The ultimate goal is to further strengthen our unique sports car brand across all model lines and with new, highly desirable models in particularly high-margin segments.”

title: MNT-Halan Opens $150m IPO Subscription on Cairo Bourse
snippet: Egypt's largest fintech float since 2021 is testing institutional appetite for high-growth emerging-market listings at a $750m valuation. The post MNT-Halan Opens $150m IPO Subscription on Cairo Bourse appeared first on The Fintech Times.
fullText:
MNT-Halan has opened subscription for the Cairo Stock Exchange listing of MNT Tech Holding, its Egyptian operating business, at EGP 24.5 per share. The base offering covers 320 million existing shares, representing a 20 per cent stake and targeting gross proceeds of approximately $150 million at a company valuation of around $750 million. The offering includes an option to upsize to 25 per cent of the company if demand justifies it. Trading is scheduled to begin on 20 October.

Mounir Nakhla, founder and CEO at MT-Halan

More than a third of the base offering has already been covered through anchor commitments from Commercial International Bank, Egypt’s largest listed private bank, and London-based asset manager Redwheel. The anchor participation is a material signal: it reduces placement risk and gives retail and institutional subscribers a reference point on pricing confidence. The issue price is set at a discount to comparable listed peers, a deliberate choice to leave secondary-market upside for new investors.

Mounir Nakhla, founder and chief executive, said the same transaction would have raised only $30 million to $40 million in early 2024, a period when Egypt’s currency crisis and foreign-exchange controls had effectively frozen inbound portfolio capital. The Egyptian pound has since been floated and an IMF programme is in place, changes that have materially improved the risk profile for foreign investors considering the market.

What the deal tests

Beyond MNT-Halan’s own fortunes, the listing functions as a live stress test for Egypt’s capital markets infrastructure and their ability to attract international institutional money. Egypt has not produced a fintech IPO of this size in five years, and the Gulf’s own IPO pipeline has decelerated in 2026 following a run of large state-linked listings in Saudi Arabia and the UAE. A clean execution and active secondary trading would encourage other late-stage Egyptian and MENA fintechs that have delayed exit plans to revisit the public-markets route.

MNT-Halan’s business model spans consumer lending, buy-now-pay-later, digital payments and e-commerce logistics, serving underbanked Egyptians who remain largely outside the formal banking system. The company traces its origins to Halan, a 2017 ride-hailing app for tuk-tuks and motorbikes in low-income urban neighbourhoods, which subsequently merged with Mounir Nakhla’s microfinance operation to build a broader financial services stack. That history of serving thin-file borrowers through non-traditional channels is central to its positioning as a financial-inclusion play for institutional investors with emerging-markets or impact mandates.

Regional context

The listing arrives alongside a cluster of other MENA fintech activity. NEOPAY has agreed to acquire a 65 per cent controlling stake in noon payments, extending consolidation in the UAE acquiring and payments infrastructure space. Saudi-based SME financing platform erad closed a $22 million Series A led by MEVP, continuing a run of mid-sized lending rounds in the Kingdom. On the institutional rails side, Mashreq Bank completed a live tokenised deposit transaction with Citi on Swift‘s blockchain ledger, and Commercial Bank of Dubai became the first bank outside Europe to join the Commercial Bank Money Token network, a sign that Gulf lenders are moving from pilot to production on wholesale digital money infrastructure.

For MNT-Halan specifically, the path from IPO to a durable public-market premium will depend on post-listing disclosures around credit quality, non-performing loan ratios and the unit economics of its lending book. International investors familiar with Egyptian consumer credit will want granular data before expanding positions in secondary trading.

title: Stablecoin startups advance payments
snippet: Entrepreneurs embracing the digital assets are pushing payments modernization forward, and bringing incumbents along too.
fullText:
Fintech entrepreneurs are using stablecoins as a means of breaking into the payments industry and driving digital modernization.

Startups such as MassPay and Rain have been forging new pathways for payments that embrace stablecoins, either incorporating or bypassing aging rails. They see an expansive opportunity ahead as they begin to make inroads.

While traditional payments players, including card network giant Visa and mega processor Fiserv, have also glommed on to the stablecoin trend, their legacy infrastructures may increase the difficulty of adapting to digital schemes.

Meanwhile, younger companies are amassing capital from venture investors and hiring employees to build stablecoin networks and accessories. The appeal for investors has been a simple one, according to Verda Ventures General Partner Alex Witt.

“The basic premise behind our fund is: sending payments should be as easy, fast, and cheap as sending a text message,” Witt said in an interview this month. “We fundamentally believe with blockchain, mobile phones, and the internet, that is completely possible.”

Witt and his business partner, Amit Chu, created a venture fund two years ago to invest in stablecoin startups and it has since drawn $40 million, he said, allowing the fund to purchase minority stakes in about two dozen companies globally. 

It’s a real change from when Witt first started to raise money for the fund in 2024 and people thought he was “completely crazy,” he said.

The Verda portfolio includes the fintech Yellow Card focused on payments in Africa as well as the blockchain infrastructure services company Capa, which operates in Latin America.

Two other companies the fund invested in have already been sold, specifically Kulipa and Beam. In addition, digital processor Stripe is circling another possible purchase, Witt said, declining to name it.

Rain evolves into stablecoin services

Rain’s holding company, Signify, began as a different business and then morphed into the one branded as Rain today. It has collected about $338 million in equity investments along the way, according to a spokesperson for the company. 

Among the private company’s investors are San Francisco investment firm Iconiq Capital, Sapphire Ventures and Coinbase’s former chief technology officer, Balaji Srinivasan, with a quarter of a billion dollars raised in the most recent round disclosed in January.

Rain provides stablecoin infrastructure services that enable corporate customers to bridge stablecoin payments so that money can move from the digital assets to traditional payment rails. Corporate clients embed the technology in their services for consumer use, letting consumers tap stablecoins in a way that’s less invisible to users. 

Early clients were crypto firms, fintechs and neobanks, sometimes in countries where the digital assets acted as a hedge against inflation, such as in Argentina. But then Rain began attracting bigger names, landing remittance provider Western Union as its first major customer last year, then a large peer, MoneyGram, and ticketing company Live Nation followed this year.

This week, Rain said it’s making a digital wallet available to consumers that will enable them to save, spend and send from a stablecoin balance that is backed by cards the company issues. For now, consumers will still custody their funds with the non-custodial wallets, but the company plans to offer custodial wallets by yearend.

Rain expands following Genius Act

Rain has grown by acquisition too. In August, Rain purchased the California payments and technology firm Ansa for an undisclosed sum. 

Now, the business employs about 150 people around the world, with a pack of them located in the New York headquarters, the company’s CEO, Farooq Malik, said in an interview last month.

The brand name Rain dawned on the founders because they saw how fast and fluid funds could be transferred using stablecoins. The same could be said for how quickly startup businesses are reacting to stablecoin developments, like the signing of the Genius Act, which created a regulatory framework for the digital assets.

President Donald Trump’s signing of that new law last year was pivotal in pushing the business forward, Malik said.

“The tipping point was really the Genius Act,” he said. “A lot of people had been waiting on the sidelines for clarity before proceeding. That gave companies and people the confidence to proceed. Consumers also have to believe this is viable.”

Now, the company aims to take another step in its evolution. It applied with the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency for a national trust charter this month, seeking the ability to offer asset custody and other related services, though they could still accept deposits or make loans. 

MassPay embraces stablecoins

Another startup growing in the stablecoin arena is Las Vegas-based MassPay, which is using the digital asset technology to streamline payments for gig workers, contractors and marketplace sellers as well as providing payout services for gaming and sports betting. It connects to local payment rails, real-time payment systems and mobile wallets.

“We've seen growing demand for stablecoins, primarily by large-scale institutions that feel comfortable due to some clearance in the regulation,” the company’s CEO, Ran Grushkowsky, said in an interview last month. Stablecoins are becoming particularly useful for speed and payments over the weekends, he explained.

The majority of MassPay’s 300 corporate clients are in North America, Grushkowsky said. They include Los Angeles-based online social platform Passes and New York-based marketplace Whop.

Last week, MassPay said it had forged a new integration with Block’s Cash App digital wallet.

MassPay’s services are offered in some 230 countries, according to the press release last December that named Grushkowsky CEO as of this year. The company has grown to process tens of billions of dollars annually, with about half of those payments moving across borders, and about 10% in stablecoins, he said.

The company is privately funded, and now employs about 54 workers, mainly in the U.S., Grushkowsky said. He declined to say how much money the owners have raised. 

As startups nudge stablecoins forward, the digital currency is slowly becoming a real possibility for payments in everyday life, Witt explained. 

“The biggest challenge, though, is that last mile of friction and localizing to consumer preferences,” Witt said. “We wanted to invest in the leaders around the world that are bridging the gap.”

title: Markets Wobble on Energy Fears as Rate Pressure Builds Globally
snippet: Brent crude above $101, India's first rate hike since 2023 and flat UK house prices are testing investor nerves heading into Q4. The post Markets Wobble on Energy Fears as Rate Pressure Builds Globally appeared first on The Fintech Times.
fullText:
Global financial markets are navigating a fresh bout of turbulence as renewed conflict in the Middle East pushes energy costs higher, forces central banks back toward tightening, and squeezes household and government balance sheets from Bristol to Paris.

Brent crude has risen back above $101 a barrel following attacks by Yemen’s Houthi rebels on targets in southern Saudi Arabia. The renewed escalation has revived fears over energy supply security and is feeding directly into inflation expectations that policymakers had hoped were receding.

Rate pressure broadens

The Reserve Bank of India raised its repo rate by 25 basis points to 5.5% this week, its first hike since February 2023. As a major energy importer, India is particularly exposed to the current fuel squeeze, and the central bank’s move signals that higher energy costs are now working their way into consumer prices fast enough to demand a policy response. Investors are watching for further central banks to follow suit.

In the UK, financial markets are pricing in a greater than 90% probability of a quarter-point Bank of England rate rise after its November meeting, with three additional increases expected through 2027. That trajectory has already drained the market of cheaper mortgage deals. Lloyds data showed UK house prices were flat in September and recorded a 0.2% quarterly decline, following the first annual fall since 2023 recorded in August. New mortgage enquiries are running at their fastest pace since February, suggesting buyers have not exited the market entirely but are proceeding with considerably more caution.

The Strait of Hormuz remains a live flashpoint. Multiple incidents involving tankers were reported by the UKMTO, the Royal Navy-led maritime security monitor, in the past week. Insurance premiums have risen sharply in response, while longer rerouting times are compounding freight costs. Those additional expenses are expected to feed through to consumer prices in the months ahead, adding to the inflationary backdrop that central banks are already struggling to contain.

Shell benefits, France wobbles

Not all market participants are absorbing losses. Shell raised its third-quarter Integrated Gas production forecast to between 740,000 and 780,000 barrels of oil equivalent per day, well above the 631,000 produced in the second quarter. Its refining margin has nearly doubled, rising from $24 per barrel in Q2 to $42 per barrel in Q3, a record level. The acquisition of ARC Resources has contributed materially to that output at a moment of acute demand.

France presents a more troubling picture. French bond yields had surged to levels not seen since the early 2000s as investor focus shifted to the country’s fiscal position. A pledge from Marine Le Pen’s National Rally party to deliver €140 billion in spending savings by 2032 offered some relief, nudging yields lower, but the political backdrop of student protests and public unrest makes that level of fiscal consolidation difficult to execute even in a favourable electoral scenario.

Susannah Streeter, chief investment strategist at Wealth Club, noted that while Wall Street appears to be taking the current environment in its stride, treating geopolitical friction as a new baseline, London is less sanguine. “The exuberance which washed over financial markets after energy prices dipped slightly has faded,” she said, “with renewed attacks in the Middle East demonstrating how a resolution to the crisis remains elusive.”

For fintech and financial services firms, the rate environment is the critical variable. Higher-for-longer rates tighten credit conditions, slow mortgage origination volumes and compress net interest margins for lenders who over-leveraged on cheap wholesale funding. The pressure is also structural for embedded-finance providers whose growth models assumed a low-rate backdrop for consumer credit products. The next Bank of England decision will set the tone for Q4 planning across the sector.

title: Triple Point Originates £55m Facility for Perch Group’s £400m Platform
snippet: Triple Point has joined a six-strong lender panel backing Blackpool-based credit management firm Perch Group under an enhanced £400m funding structure. The post Triple Point Originates £55m Facility for Perch Group’s £400m Platform appeared first on The Fintech Times.
fullText:
Triple Point has originated a £55 million facility for Perch Group, the Blackpool-headquartered credit management business, as part of an enhanced £400 million funding platform intended to support continued UK growth and technology investment. The deal, announced on 7 October 2026, adds Triple Point to a lending panel that already includes NatWest Group, Hampshire Trust Bank, Shawbrook Bank, Paragon Bank and Lloyds. Quilam Capital, an early backer, remains a material equity investor in the business.

Founded in 2016, Perch has expanded from a regional start-up into a group with more than 500 employees, over one million customers under management and assets under management exceeding £1 billion. The group operates across the full credit management lifecycle through five subsidiaries: debt purchaser Perch Capital, customer engagement specialist ACI UK, field services provider Verify, SRA-regulated law firm TM Legal and outsourced contact centre business Perch Connect. Combining those capabilities under a single ownership structure is central to the firm’s positioning.

The deal

Ellis Diamanti, head of specialty finance at Triple Point

Ellis Diamanti, head of specialty finance at Triple Point, described Perch as “a genuine UK growth story, built outside London into one of the country’s leading credit management platforms with a ten-year track record.” He added that Triple Point looks forward to supporting the business as it enters its next phase of development.

Mark Pickup, chief financial officer at Perch Group

Mark Pickup, chief financial officer at Perch Group, said the expanded funding package “provides a strong foundation for future growth as we continue investing in technology and delivering outstanding customer outcomes.” The company did not provide further detail on the specific technology projects the capital will fund, nor did it disclose the individual loan tenors or pricing within the £400 million platform.

Fieldfisher LLP acted as legal adviser to Perch Group. Hunton Andrews Kurth LLP advised Triple Point and Ashurst Perkins Coie LLP advised the senior lending syndicate.

Market context

The UK debt purchasing and credit management sector has attracted significant institutional capital over the past several years, with lenders drawn to the combination of relatively predictable cash flows from purchased debt portfolios and the regulatory clarity provided by the FCA‘s consumer credit regime. The FCA’s Consumer Duty rules, which came into full effect in 2023 and extended to closed products in 2024, have placed heightened obligations on credit management firms to demonstrate good outcomes for customers in financial difficulty. Perch’s integrated structure, which brings legal, field and contact centre capabilities in-house, is partly a response to that compliance environment: owning the full customer journey reduces reliance on third-party agents and gives the firm more direct control over conduct risk.

For Triple Point, the facility extends the firm’s specialty finance book, which sits alongside its clean energy, social housing and ventures strategies within an approximately £2.5 billion under-management platform. Specialty credit origination in the consumer debt purchasing space requires deep sector knowledge to assess portfolio quality, and the deal signals Triple Point’s appetite to compete with more established credit fund managers in this corner of the private credit market.

The breadth of the senior lending syndicate, spanning high-street names and specialist challenger banks, reflects the maturity Perch has reached as a borrower and the confidence that multiple regulated institutions have placed in its underwriting and collections model. The next indicators to watch are the pace at which Perch deploys the expanded facility into new portfolio purchases and the specific technology build-out it funds, both of which will shape whether the group can sustain AUM growth beyond the £1 billion mark.

title: Behind the Idea: Arf
snippet: Arf co-founder and CEO Ali Erhat Nalbant on why pre-funding still traps capital in cross-border payments and how on-demand settlement liquidity sets it free. The post Behind the Idea: Arf appeared first on The Fintech Times.
fullText:
Cross-border payments are getting faster, but the capital behind them has not kept pace. Payment companies still pre-fund accounts across currencies and markets so that transactions can settle, leaving money idle that could otherwise go into hiring, better services or new markets.

Ali Erhat Nalbant, co-founder and CEO at Arf

Arf, a Swiss-regulated financial institution, provides stablecoin-based settlement liquidity to licensed financial institutions, bridging fiat and stablecoin rails for B2B payment providers across the US, UK, EU, UAE, Hong Kong, Singapore and beyond.

In this Behind the Idea, Ali Erhat Nalbant, co-founder and CEO of Arf, discusses the pre-funding problem the company was set up to solve, how its model has moved from direct lending to embedded infrastructure, and where it goes next.

Tell us more about your company and its offering

Arf is a Swiss-regulated global treasury platform providing liquidity and same-day settlement for international financial institutions. We enable international payments across fiat and stablecoin rails, offering IBANs, FX, and scalable treasury infrastructure.

As payments become faster, more global and increasingly real time, liquidity has become a major bottleneck. Innovations like faster rails and stablecoins are changing how money moves, but advances in speed cannot ultimately be realised if liquidity still determines when payments settle.

Our platform changes that by providing settlement liquidity, allowing financial institutions to support payment flows, enter new markets and scale without continually raising debt or diluting equity. We bridge fiat and stablecoins to deliver same-day liquidity to B2B payment providers, so their clients can access capital at the moment they need to send, rather than after a wire clears. Put simply, we help liquidity move as freely as payments, so our clients can grow faster while putting more of their own capital to work.

What problem was your company set up to solve?

We set up the company to solve a simple but persistent problem: payment businesses need liquidity exactly when demand appears, but traditional funding is often too slow, rigid and expensive. That means companies either hold excess capital that sits idle, which diverts capital away from company growth, whether that’s hiring, investing in better services or scaling to new markets, or they risk being caught short when payment volumes spike.

For decades, financial institutions have relied on prefunding accounts across currencies and markets to ensure liquidity is available wherever and whenever a payment needs to settle. Our aim is to make liquidity work more intelligently, by providing on-demand funding that can scale with real payment activity.

Ultimately, we want to ensure capital moves to where demand exists, when it is needed, so we can eliminate the trade-off between speed and capital efficiency in cross-border payments.

Since launch, how has your company evolved?

When we started Arf, the idea was simple: payment companies shouldn’t have to lock up capital just to guarantee they can settle. What’s evolved since then is the scale and sophistication of how we deliver that.

We’ve grown from serving individual financial institutions directly to embedding liquidity into the platforms and infrastructure they already use, so on-demand funding becomes part of their existing operations rather than a separate relationship to manage.

Today, we’ve processed more than $18bn in cumulative settlement with zero defaults across more than 1,400 days, tracked live on a public dashboard, not just reported internally. Our capital turns over 4.78 times per month, reflecting how actively our liquidity is being deployed across settlement flows.

What has been the biggest challenge or most ‘tricky moment’ to overcome?

One of the biggest challenges has been operating at the intersection of financial services, regulation, and new technology. Building a blockchain-based solution for a highly regulated industry required significant effort to establish the right regulatory and operational foundations, including becoming a regulated financial institution in Switzerland.

At the same time, demand has consistently been ahead of the capital available to us. We have had to learn how to make limited working capital work as efficiently as possible while continuously improving the model. Another challenge is that there is rarely a one-size-fits-all solution in cross-border payments. Every market and financial institution has its own requirements, which means we often have to solve problems individually and keep adapting as we scale.

What are your biggest achievements or ‘proudest moment’ so far?

I’m proud of how far we’ve scaled while staying focused on the core problem we set out to solve. We’ve now processed more than $18bn in cumulative settlement with zero defaults across more than 1,400 days. But beyond the numbers, I’m particularly proud of how this model has evolved from something transactional into real infrastructure.

We’re seeing partners across payments, stablecoin infrastructure and settlement networks build on top of what we’ve created, rather than simply using Arf as another financial service. That’s a meaningful shift for us.

How would you describe the culture of your company?

I would describe our culture as entrepreneurial, persistent, and deeply focused on solving real problems. We work on complex problems where there is rarely a simple, one-size-fits-all solution, so we stay very close to our customers and keep solving problems one by one.

There is also a strong culture of resilience. Building something new in financial infrastructure takes time, and there is always another challenge to solve and another piece to put in place. We are ambitious and excited about what we are building, but we also understand that progress comes from consistently doing the hard work. At the same time, we take regulation, compliance, and accountability very seriously because we are building infrastructure for the financial system.

What’s in store for the future?

Our focus is on scaling what we have built and making liquidity more accessible for financial institutions around the world. We see significant opportunities to expand into new markets, deepen our relationships with banks and financial institutions, and support more cross-border payment corridors, particularly in regions where prefunding still ties up the most working capital.

As the market continues to evolve, we want to keep building infrastructure that makes cross-border payments faster, more transparent, and more efficient. There is still a huge amount of liquidity trapped in traditional settlement processes, and our ambition is to play a meaningful role in changing that.

title: Lumin Digital Launches Behavioural Analytics Tool for Credit Unions
snippet: Lumin Signal gives banks and credit unions pre-built visibility into user drop-off and feature discovery across 700-plus platform features. The post Lumin Digital Launches Behavioural Analytics Tool for Credit Unions appeared first on The Fintech Times.
fullText:
Lumin Digital has commercially launched Lumin Signal, a behavioural intelligence capability built natively into its digital banking platform, targeting banks and credit unions that want clearer evidence of what return their digital feature investment is generating.

The San Ramon, California company said the product arrives pre-configured across more than 100 pages and 700 features, with banking-specific terminology already applied. That means institutions can begin identifying where users abandon a process or fail to discover a feature without first running a data-team implementation project. Tags covering common banking functions such as Stop Payment, Skip-A-Pay, Remote Deposit Capture and Positive Pay are included from day one.

What Lumin Signal does

Sean Weadock, chief product and technology officer at Lumin Digital

The product groups its functionality into three components. The first is a behavioural analytics layer covering feature adoption rates, session navigation paths, funnel drop-off points and retention trends, surfaced through pre-built dashboards across eight audience segments including account tenure. The second is a Guides tool that lets administrators create in-app walkthroughs, tooltips and onboarding flows without engineering resource, publishable on the same day they are built. The third is an in-app survey function that collects user feedback at the moment of interaction rather than through a separate research programme.

Lumin illustrated the potential unit economics with one example: an eStatement adoption guide that converts 15 per cent of a 100,000-account paper-statement base, it said, could be worth approximately $540,000 a year in savings. The company did not publish independent evidence for that figure or disclose conversion rates from existing deployments.

Chief product and technology officer Sean Weadock said the capability addresses the gap between knowing what users do and understanding how they experience the platform. “Lumin Signal gives our clients a deeper understanding of how people are using digital banking, helping them identify opportunities to increase adoption, improve the experience, and generate more value for the capabilities they already have.”

Lumin positions Signal as complementary to its existing Lumin Analytics product. The two are described as distinct: Analytics provides individual, transaction-level visibility while Signal operates at the aggregate user-behaviour level and includes the in-app intervention tools. Both can be purchased independently.

Market context

The broader market for digital banking engagement and analytics tooling has grown considerably as financial institutions recognise that launching a feature and driving adoption of it are separate problems. Several established players, including Pendo, WalkMe and Amplitude, already provide product analytics and in-app guidance capabilities to enterprise software buyers, and some digital banking platform vendors have begun embedding similar functionality rather than leaving institutions to licence third-party tools.

Lumin’s pitch is that native integration removes the complexity and vendor management overhead of a standalone analytics stack. That argument carries weight with smaller credit unions and community banks, which typically lack dedicated product analytics teams. The competitive question is whether institutions that already have a preferred analytics relationship see enough friction-reduction in the native approach to switch, or whether they will treat it as a bundling decision at platform renewal time.

From a regulatory standpoint, financial institutions using behavioural data to profile user journeys must consider data governance obligations under applicable US state privacy laws, as well as internal model risk management frameworks where AI-assisted personalisation is involved. Lumin did not specify the data-retention policies or the regulatory classification of the profiling data collected through Signal, which compliance officers at prospective clients are likely to raise during procurement.

Victims of a £1.5m crypto investment fraud will recover lost funds after the FCA obtained confiscation orders against Raymondip Bedi and Patrick Mavanga.

  

            						

At a hearing at Southwark Crown Court on 28 September 2026, Raymondip Bedi was ordered to pay £603,404.28 and Patrick Mavanga £247,997.99.

Between February 2017 and June 2019, Bedi and Mavanga operated a fraudulent investment scheme, cold-calling consumers and persuading them to invest in fake cryptoasset opportunities through companies including CCX Capital and Astaria Group LLP. At least 65 investors were defrauded and lost £1,541,799.

The FCA has identified and contacted victims of the fraud and will ensure that funds recovered through the confiscation process are returned to victims.

In July 2025, following an FCA prosecution, Raymondip Bedi was sentenced to 5 years and 4 months' imprisonment and Patrick Mavanga was sentenced to 6 years and 6 months' imprisonment for their roles in the scheme.

Steve Smart, joint executive director of enforcement and market oversight at the FCA, said:

'Bedi and Mavanga defrauded investors and left them out of pocket. These orders bring victims a step closer to getting money back.

'We’ll keep coming after fraudsters and holding them to account.'

title: Fed names new payments chief
snippet: Federal Reserve Financial Services tapped Kim Robbins to succeed Mark Gould starting in November.
fullText:
The Federal Reserve’s financial services division has appointed Kim Robbins as its new top payments executive, tapping her to replace the retiring Mark Gould.

Federal Reserve Financial Services announced the appointment Thursday, picking a nearly 20-year Federal Reserve veteran to lead the division that provides payments services to financial institutions. She’ll step into the role on Nov. 16, according to the press release stating her appointment.

She has served as first vice president and chief operating officer at the Federal Reserve Bank of Kansas City since March 2024 and has been with that reserve bank in some capacity since January 2012, according to her LinkedIn profile. Prior to heading to that regional bank, she worked for Federal Reserve Financial Services as the chief of enterprise services.

In a post last week on that social media site, Robbins said she was pleased to “return ‘home’ to payments.” She also gave a nod to the work that lies ahead.

“With rapid innovation transforming the industry, it is clear to me that we are in a pivotal moment in payments,” she said. “I look forward to partnering across the Federal Reserve System and with our industry stakeholders to advance modern, secure, and resilient payment services that meet the dynamic and evolving needs of financial institutions, businesses, and the American public.”

Gould is retiring after spending the last three years with a key focus on rolling out the Fed’s instant payments system FedNow, starting in mid 2023, and trying to lure banks across the country to join the system. As of this month, the central bank has attracted just over 1,900 U.S. banks and credit unions to use the real-time payments system.

With some 8,500 financial institutions in the U.S. eligible to use the system, the Fed has a ways to go in drawing more banks and credit unions to the new service. Last month, the Fed began offering a discount program to entice financial institutions to participate in the service.

Only U.S. financial institutions can join the system, which enables them to send payments in a matter of seconds or minutes, as opposed to transactions sometimes taking days to settle. The Fed launched the instant payments system in July 2023 in the hopes of bringing smaller banks into the realm of faster payments. That followed the start of a private real-time system, the RTP Network, by bigger banks that own The Clearing House in November 2017.

In late 2024, the Fed disclosed that it cost about $246 million to operate the FedNow payments system that year, after requiring about $100 million for development in 2023, according to a report from the central bank. 

The central bank this year has also been exploring how to extend the reach of the system across international borders. Last month, the Fed said the real-time system was “on the verge” of providing cross-border transaction “support,” but then it stopped short of saying how and when. 

Robbins has leadership experience both with respect to FedNow as well as the broader Federal Reserve Financial Services, the release said. 

Specifically, the release noted that she was FedNow’s chief administrative officer, leading the “functions supporting the program’s rapid scale-up across multiple Federal Reserve Banks,” plus “strengthening the governance, risk, compliance and legal structures” for the system.

Aside from FedNow, Robbins will oversee the Fed’s retail, wholesale and securities services for financial institutions, the release noted.

Before Robbins joined the Fed, she had an early start to her career in a different kind of retail sector. She worked for seven years for the GAP and Payless ShoeSource, managing various aspects of the retail chains’ business lines.

fullText:
The FCA and Practitioner Panel annual survey of regulated firms provides valuable insights into how firms think we’re performing.

The latest survey shows 79% of firms are highly satisfied with their relationship with the FCA, up from 74% last year. The proportion of firms rating the FCA as a highly effective regulator also increased from 69% to 76%, while 75% reported high levels of trust.

Firms were most confident in our work to protect consumers (87%), ensure markets work well (85%) and enhance the integrity of the UK financial system (85%). There was a 27-percentage point increase in firms’ understanding of the Secondary International Competitiveness and Growth Objective and a 25-percentage point increase in confidence in our delivery of it.

We took on board feedback from last year’s survey and provided further guidance to help firms embed the Consumer Duty. This year, 88% of firms say they understand what we expect on supporting consumers and embedding the Duty.

The findings also provide valuable insight into where firms would like to see further progress, including on regulatory burden. We’re already simplifying reporting by removing outdated or duplicated data returns for 90% of firms.

Nikhil Rathi, chief executive of the FCA, said: 'A year into our strategy it's encouraging to see growing confidence across many areas of our work. We know there is more to do. For example, while we can’t do our job without the data firms provide, we should continue to simplify requests and make them easier to manage.'

Matt Hammerstein, chair of the FCA Practitioner Panel, said: 'This year’s survey results indicate firms continue to have broadly positive views of the FCA, including strong understanding of expectations under the Consumer Duty and significant growth in confidence in the FCA’s ability to deliver on its secondary objectives focused on growth and competitiveness.

'The Panel is encouraging the FCA to be clearer about the outcomes it expects its priorities to produce, and more vocal about the progress it is making against these, to strengthen confidence in the UK as a leading global financial centre and attractive place to invest.'

In the first year of our strategy, we've delivered an estimated £5.6bn in benefits to consumers and the economy, including launching My FCA, reducing reporting burdens to save firms around £16m annually, and introducing nearly 50 pro-growth measures to boost UK competitiveness and innovation. 

Since the survey was conducted, we’ve continued our work to deliver landmark reforms, including working with HM Treasury and the Financial Ombudsman Service to modernise the redress framework, support industry delivery of the Advice Guidance Boundary Review, regulating Buy Now Pay Later products, establishing a new regime for cryptoassets, and progressing the PISCES private markets framework.

title: Upgrade applies for ILC charter
snippet: The decade-old credit-card startup named a SoFi alum and longtime regulator as CEO of its proposed bank.
fullText:
Upgrade has applied for an industrial loan company charter with the Federal Deposit Insurance Corp. and the Nevada Financial Institutions Division, the fintech announced Monday.

“We are excited at the prospect of establishing a new bank that will advance Upgrade’s mission of bringing responsible and affordable credit to consumers,” Virginia Varela, proposed CEO of Upgrade Bank, said in a statement. 

Varela brings more than 40 years of experience in the banking sector – first, as a regulator. She spent more than two decades with the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency, and another two years as a senior bank examiner with the Federal Reserve, before specializing in bank turnarounds after the 2007-08 financial crisis, according to her LinkedIn profile.

Varela was CEO of Sacramento, California-based Golden Pacific Bank when SoFi bought the lender. She became head of SoFi’s community banking unit but left in July 2025 for Upgrade, where she is head of banking strategy.

Varela will serve on Upgrade Bank’s board alongside Upgrade co-founder and CFO Jeffrey Bogan, the company said. Raymond Specht, onetime CEO of Toyota Financial Savings Bank, will serve as an independent director on the board.

Upgrade launched roughly a decade ago offering personal loans but gradually expanded to encompass credit cards, mobile banking, auto financing and buy now, pay later. The fintech has delivered about $53 billion in credit to roughly 8.5 million customers, it said.

Upgrade counts Cross River and Celtic Bank as partners on loans, credit lines and banking services. An ILC charter would make Upgrade less dependent on those relationships.

Trump-era regulators have seen a sharp increase in new charter applications. FDIC Chair Travis Hill last year touted the ILC charter as one of a handful of ways to boost the establishment of new banks.

Rent fintech Flex and BNPL juggernaut Klarna Group applied for ILC charters in July. Car maker Stellantis received approval in May to launch an ILC. Other automotive stalwarts, including Ford and General Motors, got green lights in January. Investment firm Edward Jones followed in February. 

Some lawmakers, with backing from the banking industry, have argued that an ILC charter exempts companies from the definition of a “bank” under the Bank Holding Company Act. As long as ILCs don’t offer demand deposit accounts, they can bypass oversight by the Federal Reserve, the politicians contend.

The trade group Independent Community Bankers of America said in May that cutting the Fed out of ILC supervision “leav[es] a dangerous gap in safety and soundness oversight and introducing unnecessary systemic risk into the banking system.”

Last year, Sens. Elizabeth Warren, D-MA, and Andy Kim, D-NJ, proposed a moratorium on commercially owned ILC charters until such entities are defined as “banks” under the BHC Act.

title: Businesses view stablecoins warily
snippet: Despite the hype surrounding the digital assets, businesses remain cool to using the cryptocurrency, according to the results of a Cleveland Federal Reserve survey.
fullText:
Stablecoins aren’t going to become a disruptive force in payments in the United States anytime soon as businesses are displaying a lack of enthusiasm for the digital currency, based on a survey by the Cleveland Federal Reserve Bank.

Reasons businesses are cool to using stablecoins include lack of familiarity with the technology; satisfaction with legacy payment options; and little to no demand among customers and suppliers to use stablecoins for payment, according to the results of the Cleveland Fed’s survey in late September.

Of the survey’s 148 respondents, only one said it is currently using stablecoins. Among the remaining respondents, seven said they plan to use stablecoins in the future. The other respondents either said they weren’t sure they would use stablecoins in the future or expressed a lack of familiarity with the digital currency.

The results were somewhat surprising to Federal Reserve researchers conducting the survey as they expected more respondents to have plans to begin using stablecoins. 

“We didn’t expect the results to be as lopsided as they were,” Peter Zimmerman, a research economist for the Cleveland Fed who co-authored the report, said in summarizing the survey’s results during an interview earlier this month. 

Lack of knowledge about stablecoins is a big reason why businesses are not rushing to accept them for payment or use stablecoins for payment, according to the Cleveland Fed’s report. 

When asked what factors would influence their decision to use stablecoins, 49 respondents, about a third, cited the need for more time to observe market trends and adoption. 

While respondents were not “terribly critical” of stablecoins in their comments, many said they needed “more time to understand the technology,” Zimmerman said.

The Federal Reserve of Cleveland conducted its research in September 2025, about two months after the Genius Act became law, providing a federal regulatory framework for stablecoin payments. The Federal Reserve of Cleveland surveyed companies in the Fourth Federal Reserve District, which includes Ohio, western Pennsylvania, eastern Kentucky, and the northern panhandle of West Virginia.

One reason businesses may lack knowledge about stablecoins and potential use cases for the digital currency is that they are primarily being used for back-end settlement between banks, which keeps the technology in the background.

“What we are seeing is stablecoins being linked to cards for payments, which on the front end looks like a normal card transaction,” said Aaron McPherson, principal of AFM Consulting, in an interview this month. “Banks settle those transactions in stablecoins on the back-end between themselves, but the public doesn’t see that. What they see is the front-end of the transaction.”

Another roadblock to stablecoins becoming a mainstream payment option is the efficiency, cost effectiveness and competitiveness of existing payment options in the U.S., such as the ACH network. Some 42 survey respondents, just under a third of those surveyed, said they need more evidence stablecoins are cheaper or more efficient than other forms of payment.

“Any new payment option clearly has to be better than the existing options to break the inertia,” McPherson said. “There is a cost of acceptance for stablecoins, like other payment options, but stablecoins don’t have a clear economic advantage over many established payment methods yet.”

Lack of demand from customers to pay with stablecoins is also a barrier for businesses to accept or pay with stablecoins. Among respondents to the Cleveland Fed’s survey, 50, or about a third, said consumer demand to accept stablecoins for payment is a key factor influencing their decision to use stablecoins.

“To get people to want to pay with stablecoins, they need an inducement to do so, such as earning rewards,” McPherson said.

McPherson likens the situation to the chicken and egg scenario with any new payment option: acceptance drives usage and vice versa. “Inducing demand to spend stablecoins will boost acceptance,” McPherson added.

Despite the many headwinds facing stablecoins as a payment option, the best use case for the digital currency is cross-border payments, say some industry consultants. Using stablecoins for cross-border payments enables funds to move directly between the sender’s and recipient’s digital wallet, which reduces the number of parties involved in the transaction, lowers fees and speeds the transaction.

“In the U.S., stablecoins are largely a niche payment option and their best use case is cross-border payments,” Tony DeSanctis, vice president for Cornerstone Advisors, said in an interview this month. “Businesses that have a lot of international clients is where we will see activity.”

If businesses are going to overcome their lack of enthusiasm for using stablecoins, they need an answer to the question of how stablecoins will improve operations.

“Businesses need to be educated about what the technology is capable of, [to understand] whether it can disrupt the current state of payments and find the niche where it can serve,” DeSanctis said. “No one knows for sure what technology will be the next market disruptor, but we haven’t seen enough of stablecoins to make that distinction.”
